memories.memory_text: I screamed at Pedro, smacking him with my gloves until I was out of breath, yelling about his sister because he thought it was funny to harass someone.
After the guys started applauding, I looked around and just stormed off, kicking a piece of wood at one of them before brushing past Walter toward the exit.

I told Walter I don't like to waste time, then kissed him—right there on the couch—because asking about his damage was enough; talking more would've just been pretending we didn't both want the same thing.

I remember looking at that bus map on his wall, how bare the place was, and then just knowing—something in his eyes when he sat down, the way he held himself—that it wasn't shyness, it was damage, and I called it out.
I laughed and nudged Walter’s butt with my foot after he made that dumb joke about me not being a dyke—he was shy, but I could tell he was pleased.

I told him I wanted to stay the night, then said it straight—'I like to sleep with a man after we fuck'—and when he didn’t answer, I asked if I’d said something wrong, my voice cracking just a little.
I flicked a straw wrapper at Walter while he was eating, just to break the silence and see what he’d do.
I saw Walter crack a smile after he flicked a wrapper back without looking up, and I had to stifle a laugh.
I called out to Walter and waved him over from my Jeep. I don’t know if he’ll come, but I had to try.

I was halfway through my burger, just trying to eat, and then Walter turns his napkin into a damn rabbit puppet that starts nodding at me—next thing I know, I’m laughing so hard I almost choke on my food.
I sank two balls in one shot and saw the look on Walter’s face—he knew he was getting beat, and I wasn’t hiding how much I liked it.
He gave me a quarter, and without thinking, I kissed him on the cheek—then just turned and lined up my next shot like it was nothing.
I told Walter I fucked my best friend's husband, watching his face the whole time, but he didn't say a word—just lay there like a stone.
After I admitted what I did, I asked him what was wrong, and he asked me about the worst thing I'd ever done—like he was measuring my guilt against something he couldn't say.
I was driving, cigarette in hand, wind hitting my face, and I couldn't stop the tears—then the horns blared and I realized I'd frozen at the light.

I was standing by the wood chips, just trying to catch a breath with a cigarette, and when Walter came near, I looked at him—really looked—hoping he’d meet my eyes, but he just kept pushing that cart like I wasn’t even there.
I saw Walter standing there at the bus stop, just another shadow in the dusk, and I didn’t look back when I drove past him.
I held those dead leaves in my hand and just stared at them—then I told the plant, 'Don't die on me, you little shit,' and blasted it with water like it was personal.
After spraying the plant, I saw myself in the window—just standing there, cigarette in hand—and I couldn't look away. I don't even know who that person was.
I stood at Walter's door and asked him if he wanted to go for a ride—just like that, no warning. I could see him trying to figure me out, tucking his shirt in like it mattered.

I told Walter about my father—how he could name every fish in the lake and spin a story for each, but still drank himself to death. I hated fishing, but I loved those stories, and saying it out loud made my chest tight.
I shoved Walter and screamed at him to change my mind, to try—really try—and when he finally broke and told me about losing his wife and daughter, I saw something real in his face.

I told Walter, flat out, that all three of my brothers abused me—just like that, lying there in his arms, after he asked about the odds of me surviving with them. I said it quiet, like it was just another fact, but my hands were shaking when I lit the cigarette.

I told Walter I love my brothers, even after what they did. He said 'No you don't,' but I told him again—I love all of them. When he asked if I ever confronted them, I laughed because the idea seemed absurd.
I told Walter to move in with me, right there in his kitchen, after he started acting weird about us. I remember saying it was a fucking good idea, like it should’ve been obvious.
When he said we should quit, I just said 'Fine,' got up, put my jacket on, and left. I didn’t look back, but I remember the door clicking shut behind me—solid, like it meant something.

I set the ivy down hard on the table and told Walter to give it a little water, go easy on the sun, and actually notice it once in a while—like it mattered. Then I told him he was such an asshole and kissed him before he could say anything stupid.

After I kissed him and walked away, he called my name and tossed me this small carved figure. I caught it, looked at it for a long time, then at him—he said it was cedar, that he made it for me. I just smiled, but I felt it.
I was trying to turn around to face him, to feel close, but he kept holding me in place, wouldn't let me move or touch him—even when I reached back, he caught my hand like it meant nothing.

memories.memory_text: I remember the click of the keys as they typed my name, the date—02/25/02—into that screen. My face on the blue background, frozen, like it wasn’t even me anymore.
I counted each step—heel to toe—until I reached one hundred and twenty, then touched the school entrance. The frost was sharp under my shoes, and I said, 'How about that!?' to the hawk above.
A red ball bounced to my feet, and I heard children laughing—but when I looked, there was nothing. Then just the squeak of an empty swing moving in the wind, back and forth, no one on it.
I opened the notebook, closed it, then opened it again, staring at the blank page before finally starting to write.
I was walking to the bus stop with the others when I heard her shout. I saw Vicki in her Jeep, waving at me like we were supposed to know each other out here.
I handed her a quarter after she sank two balls—she was beating me bad, and I just gave her the coin without a word, feeling the weight of the loss but also something close to amusement.
She kissed me on the cheek—sudden, soft—then walked away to take her next shot, leaving me standing there, not moving, the warmth of it lingering more than I expected.
I told her I molested little girls, and she laughed at first, like it was some kind of joke, until she realized I wasn’t.
I opened the door and saw Carlos struggling with the table on the landing, and I asked him what he was doing—my voice came out tight, like something in my chest had locked.
I made that table for Carlos and Annette’s wedding, poured my heart into it, and she wanted to throw it out like scrap wood.
I looked at her, slammed my locker shut, and walked past without a word.
I wiped my mouth and stood up when Mary-Kay started talking about the day being beautiful. I said I had another load coming in.
Prison is time. That's it. You think time, you feel time, you hear time. Your heart doesn't beat to live, it just beats... time.
I used to tell myself the girls seduced me. But I don't believe that anymore. I said it out loud—that it was a lie I told myself.
I held her close and said being here with me was crazy—like it wasn’t safe, like I wasn’t safe. I told her the odds were against me, that most men like me end up back there.
I got on the bus and looked for Candy's car like I always did, but the spot was empty—just pavement where her white Volvo should’ve been.
I got off the bus with the others, blending in, just another face in the crowd. I followed a girl.
She gave me a look — just for a second, our eyes met before she turned the corner. I don't know why, but I started walking after her.
I was close, just a few feet away, when the salesman spoke. I turned and saw the guard — suddenly I couldn't breathe, and she was gone. I ran.
I told her it wasn't a good idea, us seeing each other—then she said we should live together. I said I’ve got problems, and that we should call it quits.
She just stood up, put her fork down, pulled on her jacket, and left. I looked at the door, then said I was glad—but I wasn’t sure I meant it.

I opened my locker and saw that picture of a girl on a swing, the one with the red mark through it and those words—'WE'RE WATCHING YOU'—written underneath. I tore it down fast and looked around, but no one noticed, not one of them.
I told Carlos I was busy in July, and when he kept pushing, I said maybe I'm not a good man—maybe I'm bad inside and always will be.
I held her hips and moved her slowly on my lap, not letting her turn or touch me—I kept her hand at her side when she reached back. I just needed it this way.

I watched Candy work the boy like a match—patting his head, flashing the M&Ms, playing it cool. I called it round one to Candy, like it was a game I understood, like I knew the moves before they happened.

The boy looked around, saw no one, and crossed the street. I said it plain: 'The cherub gets in the car.' Then I repeated it—'The boy gets in the car'—like if I said it again, it might mean something different. It didn’t.
I was sitting by the window, just watching, and then her hands were on my shoulders—sudden, too close. I flinched and told her not to do that, not to sneak up behind me like that.

I looked through her binoculars at the nest in the birch tree—three small starling chicks moving weakly, beaks open. I handed them back and asked if she always carries them, trying to keep my voice steady.

She closed her eyes and made a soft, bright sound—'Cheery! Cheerily!'—shy at first, then clearer. When she finished, I said, 'That was terrific,' and meant it, though I wasn't sure if I meant the sound or the moment.
I looked down and saw the blood on my hands, still warm, and then Candy was on the ground moaning—I couldn’t move.
Robin lowered the binoculars and stared right at me—like she could see through everything I was trying to hide.
I reached for her arm, and she pulled away before shouting at me—then just stared, silent and hard—before walking off without a word. I stood there, watching her get in the car and leave.
